lesson_title: One Formula, Every Pattern Question: Linear Patterns
hook_text: Prove 163 will NEVER show up in this sequence — one line of algebra, case closed.
clip_script: Is one hundred and sixty-three a term of this sequence? Suppose it is, and chase its position: five n minus one equals one hundred and sixty-three, so five n equals one hundred and sixty-four, so n equals one hundred and sixty-four fifths — thirty-two comma eight. But positions are whole: the sequence has a thirty-second term and a thirty-third term with nothing in between. So the conclusion, written the way markers expect it: one hundred and sixty-three is not a term of the sequence, because n equals one hundred and sixty-four over five is not a natural number. The broken n is not an error in your algebra — the broken n is the proof itself.
visual_style: Terms of the sequence lighting up along a number line in steps of five, a searchlight sweeping for 163 and finding only a gap between positions 32 and 33, the fraction 164/5 slamming down as the verdict.
pacing: Steady build through the equation, hard beat on 'the broken n is the proof itself'.
